title: Screening Alert Management Tools with AI
summary: What to evaluate in AI screening alert tools: triage, false-positive claims, OFAC calibration, and an audit trail you can replay.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** A screening alert management tool is a control only when a later reviewer can replay why an alert was closed. The list entry, the fields compared, the disposition, and the test of the software all have to sit in the record. A[SAS survey with KPMG](https://www.sas.com/en_us/news/press-releases/2025/february/anti-money-laundering-survey-ai-machine-learning.html) of 850 ACAMS members, published on February 25, 2025, found that only 18 percent of respondents have AI or machine learning in production.


## What an alert management tool is actually for


An alert management tool exists to record a decision, not to hold a queue. Screening software compares a name, an address, or a payment party with a list and opens an alert when the comparison crosses a line. The management problem starts there: who takes the alert, which evidence they use, how they dispose of it, and whether someone else can follow the same path later.


OFAC's[Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments](https://ofac.treasury.gov/media/16331/download?inline) describes what those controls have to accomplish. They identify, interdict, escalate, report, and keep records. The framework also tells an institution to calibrate screening software to its risk profile and to test that software routinely. A faster queue with a thinner file misses that second obligation.


Alert volume is why buyers start the search. A[LexisNexis Risk Solutions study with Forrester](https://risk.lexisnexis.com/global/en/about-us/press-room/press-release/20240221-true-cost-of-compliance-us-ca) , published February 21, 2024, found that screening alerts had increased at 83 percent of mid-size and large firms and at 87 percent of small firms. That rise is a direct reason[screening alerts pile up](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/why-are-screening-alerts-piling-up) faster than review capacity. Volume explains the backlog. A shorter queue is an operational result. A close that a later person can replay is the compliance result.


Apply the test to a closed alert an examiner might pull. Read the record without opening the screening engine again. The record should show the list entry as it stood that day, the party screened, the fields that agreed or contradicted, the disposition, and who accepted it. A status code and a timestamp show that the alert moved. They leave the reason unstated.


## Most teams are not running this in production


Production use of AI for screening alert work is still uncommon. The SAS and KPMG survey of 850 ACAMS members found that only 18 percent have AI or machine learning in production. Respondents were specific about the job they wanted done. Twenty-eight percent said triaging high- and low-risk alerts is where AI or machine learning offers the most value, and 38 percent named reducing false positives and negatives.


Triage decides which alerts a person should see first and which ones a documented process can close. Reducing false positives and false negatives is the quality of that split. Production means the tool touches live alerts, the institution can reconstruct closed cases, and someone has tested it against the institution's own names, lists, and customer book. Ranking a vendor sample is not production.


Software that looked accurate on a generic file can still be set wrong for a remittance product, a correspondent book, or a customer base full of short transliterated names. List updates change which names alert. A proof of concept drifts when the lists or the customer mix move, unless the institution reruns a test it owns.


Programs trying to[reduce screening alert review time](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/reduce-screening-alert-review-time) should ask which minutes actually disappear. Minutes fall when the comparison is assembled before a person opens the case, and when the reason is written as the case closes. Minutes also fall when alerts are suppressed and nobody samples what was held back. The second path leaves a quieter queue and an untested miss rate.


## A name match is not a decision


A name match is not a decision. A similarity score opens the alert. Closing it requires a judgment about whether the screened party and the list entry are the same person or entity.[Sanctions screening name matching](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/sanctions-screening-name-matching) is a stack of algorithms, thresholds, and secondary identifiers. The score starts the file. The disposition ends it.


[LexisNexis Risk Solutions](https://risk.lexisnexis.com/global/en/insights-resources/article/entity-resolution-redefining-false-positive-problem) describes institutions struggling under false-positive rates of 95 percent or more in a screening context, and it footnotes that figure to KPMG. At that rate the ordinary alert is a name collision. Stacking a second score on the first does not decide the case. The decision compares identifiers: date of birth, nationality, address, a registration or identification number, and whether the hit landed on a primary name or a weak alias. Payment messages often carry fewer of those fields than a customer record. The tool should show that thin data instead of covering it with another number.


A close that will still read well later cites a contradiction, and it treats a blank as a blank. A different date of birth, nationality, or registration number can support a clear when the list entry actually contains the field. A missing date of birth is not a mismatch. Calling the name common is a weak reason on its own, because common names are where a true match is easiest to dismiss. The write-up should name the fields checked, the values on each side, and the conclusion those values support. Escalation uses the same structure when the fields are too thin, when they agree, or when a weak alias hits a higher-risk party.


Software that recommends a clear has to leave that comparison in the case, in language a second analyst can follow without rerunning the search. A confidence label with no fields cannot be replayed. Neither can a note that the alert fell under a threshold after a rescore, unless the record shows which fields moved and which threshold applied. The replay has to use the list version current on the day the alert opened.


## What to demand before you buy


Demand a record a person can replay before the first demo. Four capabilities separate a control from a queue product: triage, match logic, the disposition record, and testing.[Comparing sanctions screening software](https://sphinxhq.com/blog-posts/best-sanctions-screening-software-2026) means scoring the matching engine and the case workflow apart. A strong matcher with a weak close still fails a sample of disposed alerts.


Capability What good looks like What a weak claim sounds like


Triage The tool lines up the list entry and the customer or payment record before an analyst opens the alert, and it separates contradictions from thin or consistent matches. A reduction percentage with no denominator, no list set, and no sample of alerts the tool withheld.


Match logic The institution can see which fields moved the score and can rerun transliterations, reordered names, and short-name collisions from its own book. "The model understands context," with no fields and no step a reviewer can repeat.


Disposition record The case stores the list version, the values compared, the recommendation, and the acceptance, so a later reader can follow the close. "Full audit trail" that turns out to be status changes and a note saying the name is common.


Testing The institution owns a set of true matches, near-matches, and known clears, reruns it after list and model changes, and keeps the results. A one-time proof of concept on the vendor's file, or a dashboard of alerts closed per hour.


Triage should finish before an analyst opens the alert. Consistent identifiers, and weak aliases on higher-risk parties, should arrive with the comparison already built. A weak pitch leads with a reduction figure and skips the denominator. Ask whether the count is alerts withheld, alerts cleared after review, or both, which lists and customer segment produced it, and whether anyone sampled withheld alerts for true matches.


Match logic has to be inspectable, or the institution cannot calibrate it. A buyer should see which fields entered the score and how secondary identifiers moved it. Rerun a transliteration, a reordered surname, a corporate suffix change, and a short name that collides with ordinary customers, once on a sparse payment message and once on a customer record with an identification number. If the vendor cannot show the step behind a recommendation, the institution cannot test the tool when the lists change.


The disposition record is what an examiner reads. Store the list identifier, the screened party, the fields and values, the recommendation, who accepted it, and the list version from the day the alert opened. A log of status changes proves sequence, not a reason. A note that the name is common fails the same test. If the explanation ages out of the workflow tool, the institution kept a queue history and lost the decision.


Testing is how calibration survives go-live. Build a set the institution owns: confirmed matches, deliberate near-matches, and known clears from its own customers and payments. Rerun it after list updates, threshold changes, and model changes, and file the results with the change. Alerts closed per hour are not a detection test. Ask whether the right names still surface and whether recommended clears still rest on contradictions in the data. Reviewers should be able to add cases the vendor has not seen.


A model or rule change must not overwrite the explanation that was true on the day of the close. A person must also be able to reject a recommendation, with the rejection stored beside it and supported by its own reason. Automation that cannot be refused leaves the institution defending a decision it was not allowed to challenge.


## Where Sphinx fits


Sphinx agents review screening alerts inside the systems analysts already use, document the reason for each disposition, and leave the audit record in place. No API project required. The screening engine still produces the hit. The agent assembles the comparison and writes the close so a later reviewer can replay it.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What should an AI screening tool do before an analyst opens the alert?


Before an analyst opens the alert, the tool should assemble the list entry, the customer or payment record, and the fields that agree or contradict, then attach those facts to a recommended disposition. The analyst should see the comparison, not a bare score or a rank in the queue. A tool that only sorts alerts still leaves the decision unwritten.


### How do I compare false-positive claims from two screening vendors?


Compare the denominator, the lists, and the population, not the headline rate. Ask whether the figure counts alerts withheld before review, alerts cleared after review, or both, and whether the vendor checked a sample of withheld alerts for true matches. A claim that cannot be rerun on the institution's names, against its lists, is not comparable to another vendor's number.


### Does OFAC expect a person to review every sanctions match?


OFAC's Framework for OFAC Compliance Commitments judges a program on controls that identify, interdict, escalate, report, and keep records, and on screening software calibrated to the risk profile and tested routinely. Those commitments do not set a rule that a person must open every name match. A person still has to be able to replay why a match was cleared, and the institution still has to test that the software fits its risk.


### What has to be logged when software recommends clearing an alert?


Log the alert, the list entry and list version, the customer or payment record, the fields that supported the clear, the recommendation, and the person who accepted it. A later reviewer should reach the same conclusion from that record without rebuilding the search. A timestamp and a status code do not meet that standard.
